h1: Studying brewing abroad or in India
title: Studying Brewing Abroad or in India | Craft Beer School
desc: Brewing degrees abroad, professional exams, Indian science degrees and short courses compared, so you can choose a route that fits your time and money.
teaser: A brewing degree in Germany or Scotland, a science degree at home or a short course first. Each one suits a different person.
standfirst: There is no single right way to study brewing. The choice comes down to how much time and money you have, where you want to work and how sure you are that brewing is for you.
sections: Start with what you want to do

Brewing education serves very different goals. Someone aiming to run quality at a large brewery needs deep science. Someone opening a brewpub needs practical brewing and business sense. Someone who simply wants to test the idea needs a low cost way to find out.

Decide which of these you are before you look at prospectuses. Our comparison of a brewing degree versus a short course covers the trade off in more detail.

Germany has the longest academic tradition. Weihenstephan, part of the Technical University of Munich, offers brewing and beverage technology degrees. VLB in Berlin and Doemens in Munich run respected programmes and shorter courses. In the UK, Heriot-Watt University in Edinburgh offers postgraduate study in brewing and distilling. In the United States, the Siebel Institute and the University of California, Davis are long established.

These are serious qualifications that are widely recognised. They are also expensive once you add travel, living costs and time away from work. Some degree programmes expect the local language. Check entry requirements, visas and current fees directly with each institution.
Professional exams you can sit without moving

The Institute of Brewing and Distilling sets a ladder of exams, from the General Certificate in Brewing up to the Diploma and Master Brewer. You study largely on your own and sit exams at approved centres in many countries. They suit people already working in a brewery who want a recognised credential without leaving their job.

See our brewing certifications guide for how these compare with tasting qualifications.

India does not yet have a widely recognised dedicated brewing degree. Most Indian brewers with formal training studied food technology, microbiology, biotechnology or chemical engineering, then learned brewing on the job, through IBD exams or abroad. That is a perfectly good route. The science transfers directly and large breweries hire from these courses.

What a science degree does not give you is brewhouse practice. A first-year student can recite the chemistry of starch conversion yet never have run an iodine test on a real mash to check it has finished. Pair the degree with an internship and some hands-on brewing.
Short courses as the first step

Short courses cost a fraction of a degree and fit around a job. A good one teaches the full process, from malt and mashing to fermentation, hygiene and quality, by people who have brewed commercially. It will not make you a head brewer. It will tell you quickly whether you want to spend years becoming one.

For many people in India the sensible order is a short course, then an internship, then a decision about a degree or IBD exams. You spend real money only once you know.

Look for a course that includes assignments you actually do, such as designing a recipe, calculating a target gravity or planning a cleaning routine. Watching lectures teaches vocabulary. Doing the work is what shows you whether the process makes sense to you. Ask whether classes are live so you can put questions to the tutor. Ask too whether recordings are kept for the weeks you miss.

Compare total cost, not tuition alone. A degree abroad means fees, flights, visas, rent and a year or more without a salary. IBD exams mean exam fees and books, but you keep your job. A short course costs the least and fits around work. For reference, our own Brewing Fundamentals course is four weeks of live weekend classes for ₹5,999.

Think too about what each route does for your network. Studying abroad gives you classmates who go on to work in breweries around the world. Studying in India gives you a network that hires in India. Either can matter more than the certificate.

Finally, be honest about your current level. If you have never brewed a batch, a two year degree is a big bet on an idea you have not tested. Brew at home, take a short course, spend a few weeks in a working brewery. Then decide.

Ask three things of any programme. Who teaches it? Have they brewed for a living? How much practical brewing is included? Where do its graduates work now? A course that cannot answer the last question clearly is a risk, whatever its brochure says.
faqs: Do I need to study abroad to become a brewer in India?
No. Many Indian brewers trained through science degrees, short courses, IBD exams and work in breweries. A degree abroad helps for some senior and technical roles but is not required.
Can I take IBD brewing exams from India?
The IBD runs exams at approved centres in many countries. Check the institute's current list of centres and exam dates before you plan your study.
Which Indian degree is best for a brewing career?
Microbiology, biotechnology, food technology and chemical engineering all lead naturally into brewing. Choose the one whose subjects interest you, then add practical brewing.
